notes.text: The most obvious function of language is to communicate information. This is known as the {{23:...}} use of language. However, there are other situations where language is used without any exchange of information. For example, {{24:...}} uses of language, when we express negative sensations such as {{25:...}} or frustration or positive sensations such as an appreciation of art or affection for friends and family. We also use language without exchanging information when we engage in what Malinowski called phatic communication.

This type of language use helps to avoid potential {{26:...}} and to keep people's relationships friendly and relaxed. Examples include enquiring about somebody's health or when we discuss the weather.

passage.title: Linguistics expert David Crystal considers some functions of language

paras.text: The question 'Why do we use language?' seems hardly to require an answer. 'To communicate our ideas' is the usual answer to the question and, indeed, this must surely be the most widely recognised function of language. Whenever we tell people about ourselves and our circumstances, we are using language in order to exchange facts and opinions. This use of language is often called ideational, and is found in any spoken or written interaction where people wish to learn from each other. But it would be wrong to think of it as the only way in which we use language. Language scholars have identified several other functions where the communication of ideas is a marginal or irrelevant consideration.

Consider a situation in which Mr X carefully leans his walking stick against a wall, but it falls over. He tries again, and it falls a second time. Mr X curses the walking stick. How should we classify this function of language? It cannot be 'communication of ideas', for there is no-one else in the room. Here we have one of the commonest uses of language: a means of getting rid of our nervous energy when we experience stressful situations. It is the clearest case of what is often called an emotive function of language, which is most commonly used when we are in a frustrated state or feel anger. But there are also many emotive utterances of a positive kind, such as our involuntary verbal reactions to beautiful art or scenery, or our articulation of affection towards others. The most common such utterances consist of conventional words or phrases (such as 'Oh dear') and the semi-linguistic noises often called interjections (such as 'Wow!').

Take another situation in which Mrs P sneezes violently, Mrs Q says 'Bless you' and Mrs P says 'Thank you'. This hardly seems to be a case of language being used to communicate ideas, but rather to maintain comfortable relationships between people. Its sole function is to provide a means of preventing possible embarrassment to either party. No factual content is involved. Similarly, the uses of such phrases as 'Good morning' or 'Pleased to meet you', and ritual exchanges about health or the weather, do not 'communicate ideas' in the usual sense. This function of language, which arises out of the basic human need to signal friendliness - or, at least, lack of enmity - was first referred to as phatic communication by the anthropologist Bronislaw Malinowski (1884- 1942).

There are many situations where the most apparent reason for language being used is for the rhythmic or phonetic effect it has on the users or listeners. We can group together here such different cases as the rhythmical litanies of religious groups. The persuasive cadences of political speechmaking, and the voices of individuals singing in the kitchen or bath. Perhaps the clearest cases are the largely nonsensical nature of many traditional children's rhymes and playground language games, together with the lyrics of popular songs, and the range of phonetic effects which can be encountered in poetry.

Take the case of a solicitor preparing advice for a client. He pulls down an old book of judgements from his shelf, and reads an account of a case which took place 25 years ago. What use of language is this? At first sight, it would appear to be ideational; but the situation in which the communication takes place is quite different in several respects. When data is stored away, it is impossible to foresee who is likely to need it in the future and for what purpose; indeed, much of the material may never be referred to again. There is therefore no 'dialogue' element in the communication. Accordingly, when language is used in this way, it is very different from that used in everyday conversation; in particular, it displays a much greater degree of organisation, impersonality, and explicitness.

People often feel the need to verbalise their mental processes. Perhaps the most common such use of language is found when people perform mathematical calculations 'in their head'. Very often, this supposedly 'mental act' is accompanied by a verbal commentary. If asked why they do it, they reply that it helps their concentration. Authors often make similar remarks about the need to get a first draft down on paper, in order to see whether what they have written corresponds to what they had in mind. The French essayist Joseph Joubert (1754-1824) once said: 'We only know what we meant to say after we have said it.'.

Crowds attending events such as presidential re-elections often repeatedly shout phrases such as 'Four more years!'. What kind of language is this? Such language is hardly informative for those who use it, but it plainly has an important role in helping us feel we are members of a group; in this case, those who hold the same political views. Many public situations display language which unites rather than informs, such as the chanting of fans at a football match. Our use of language can tell our listener or reader a great deal about ourselves, by the signalling of who we are and what our alliances are.
